analysis.one_liner: Restricts credit card network fees and merchant rules, and requires public disclosure of swipe fees.
analysis.headline: The bill drew bipartisan support and a House committee hearing in October 2009, but was never voted on and died when the 111th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have rewritten the rules that credit and debit card networks impose on stores. It would bar networks from charging merchants higher fees on premium rewards cards, stop networks from restricting how merchants display prices, steer customers, route transactions, or set minimum card-acceptance volumes, and require the Federal Trade Commission to police network rules that are unfair, deceptive, or anticompetitive. It would also require the Federal Reserve to publish what each network charges, and card statements to show those fees to cardholders.
analysis.who_benefits: Small and large merchants who accept cards, who would gain fee caps on premium cards, freedom to steer customers to cheaper payment methods, and full disclosure of the secret contract rules binding them. Cardholders would benefit indirectly if merchants' fee savings show up in prices, and directly from seeing network fees on their statements.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Merchants who accept cards, and cardholders

how_it_helps.text: Prohibits networks from charging merchants higher interchange or processing fees on premium rewards cards than on ordinary cards, removing a fast-growing fee category.

Bans network rules that restrict merchants from displaying prices as they choose, steering customers to a preferred payment method, choosing how transactions are routed for processing, or setting minimum and maximum amounts for card use.
Bars networks from imposing minimum transaction-volume requirements on merchants, or charging fees or taking adverse action when a merchant falls short.
Requires networks to disclose to merchants their complete operating rules and contract terms before binding them, without restricting how merchants use that information.
Directs the FTC to write regulations ensuring network rules and terms are neither unfair nor deceptive to consumers and merchants, nor anticompetitive, and to review them regularly.

Directs the Federal Reserve to collect and publish complete information on the interchange, processing, and other fees each network charges, and adds those fees to cardholders' account disclosures and statements.

analysis.who_pays: Card networks (such as Visa and Mastercard) and the banks that issue their cards, which would lose the ability to charge premium fees and hide contract terms, and would face public disclosure of their fee schedules. Banks might respond by trimming cardholder rewards or raising card fees to recover interchange revenue.

drawbacks.text: Card-issuing banks could offset lost interchange revenue by raising annual fees or cutting rewards programs, shifting part of the cost back to cardholders, who would not pay interchange directly.
The bill would let merchants set minimum and maximum amounts for card payments, which could inconvenience consumers who want to use a card for small purchases.
New FTC rulemaking and Federal Reserve data collection would add compliance and disclosure burdens on networks, processors, and banks.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core benefit is real: interchange fees are baked into the prices all shoppers pay, and the bill would expose them and loosen network control over merchants. The main honest cost is that banks might claw back revenue through cardholder fees or reduced rewards, so the savings for consumers depend on competition passing them through. The transparency provisions are low-risk; the fee caps on premium cards are where the trade-off sits.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the House Financial Services Committee, got one hearing in October 2009, and never received a committee vote or a floor vote before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Peter Welch introduced the bill on May 13, 2009, and it was referred to the House Committee on Financial Services.
The committee held a hearing on the bill on October 8, 2009, but took no further action.
Twenty-one representatives cosponsored the bill: 17 of 253 House Democrats and 4 of 178 House Republicans.
No committee markup, committee vote, or floor vote was ever scheduled, and the bill died at the end of the 111th Congress in January 2011.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Card networks and the banks that issue their cards are better off: no limits were placed on premium-card fees, no merchant protections were enacted through this bill, and interchange fees and contract terms remained undisclosed in the ways the bill would have required.

for.name: Peter Welch
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and gathered 21 cosponsors from both parties.

against.name: Barney Frank
against.what_they_did: Held one hearing on the bill but never brought it to a committee vote or to the House floor.

against.name: Credit card networks and large card-issuing banks
against.what_they_did: Opposed restrictions on interchange fees and network merchant rules during the 2009-2010 payment-fee fights.

sides.party_line_note: Sponsorship was bipartisan but modest: of 21 cosponsors, 17 were Democrats and 4 were Republicans, and the bill never reached a floor vote where party positions would be recorded.

industries.note: Their revenue comes from interchange fees that merchants pay and recover through prices charged to all customers. The bill would cap premium-card fees, void rules that lock merchants in, and force public disclosure of fee schedules and contract terms.
Interchange fees flow to issuing banks and fund rewards programs. The bill would expose these fees on cardholders' statements and ban premium-card fee premiums, threatening a major revenue stream.

industries.industry: Retailers and small businesses that accept cards
industries.note: They would gain freedom to steer customers, route transactions, and set card minimums, plus full disclosure of the network rules binding them. Their savings could also lower prices for consumers.
Covered as network agents, they would face the same disclosure and conduct rules, but merchant steering and routing rights could open processing competition that some processors could win.
